item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable judgment framework, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark but the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships went everywhere, and the country grew so rich that its paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada around the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British Navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot do without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly collapsed.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having its cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own vital point. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast. Oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other, throwing up solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is one thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to feed themselves.

25:50 Every round of technology dividends needs new institutions to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is nice it raises my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era came with the Homestead Act, the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the 20th century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley tilts toward the tech Hamiltonians
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and hit with everything once struck. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the room. Mead says the new species really worth watching is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with more equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he visited a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later he went again, and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones alongside hunting the enemy drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. Things flip every six months. The bitter irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution — legacy equipment turns from advantage into relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no big battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On ‘will the mainland attack Taiwan’, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it will cross the threshold — a failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for instance requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade — actions sufficient to change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine and reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculus has to add Japan in, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will completely reset it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, an IV line is placed and two blood pressure cuffs are put on (arm and right leg), with EKG, EEG and EMG hooked up. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant (such as succinylcholine) is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are already relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 How electrodes are placed, and why the right side first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it has fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function is in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During treatment, doctors switch based on the patient's side effects and response: if bilateral side effects are too much, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral isn't working well enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then probe upward from a low dose until a seizure appears. But treatment isn't just about reaching the threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. This dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. If in one session a patient's seizure doesn't occur or doesn't last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, or even longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter changes: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over consecutive treatments. Two, large fluctuations in hormones such as ACTH, prolactin and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanisms may also differ across diseases (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so for now we can only keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key data are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms completely gone) of 50%-60%, and response rates (symptoms clearly improved) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the maximum remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate in half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression combined with severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Among side effects, memory problems draw the most concern
ECT's most troublesome side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive functions actually improve in the long term — possibly from the depression improving. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) mostly recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, so many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it usually affects recall of the most recent months or even years after treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a often-misidentified, potentially fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often simply classified as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological disease can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely motionless and mute, and may show posturing or waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and are immobile for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (the 'Brain on Fire' case) mentioned earlier developed catatonia; immunotherapy and lorazepam both failed, and she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is difficulty finding a treatment site. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across states for care are not few, especially in cases of infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. So improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often don't recognize catatonia and don't dare or don't think to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is also part of his daily work.

item.title: The US Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the line of American public school students' constitutional rights; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the line of American public school students' constitutional rights; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.

Each case gets five or six minutes covering the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp in one sitting where the lines fall on speech, corporal punishment and searches in US public schools.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse first
Can students really invoke the First Amendment in class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II pushed more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6 to 3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe, nor make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students hold some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer text is ruled unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added "Under God" to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short, non-denominational prayer, with each district deciding whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer let students opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6 to 1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted establishing religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest US involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusal to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7 to 2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or provably imminent substantial interference with teaching, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said: public schools may not be totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host says on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds pretty absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be cut
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still allow the interviewees to be identified, and a divorce story that named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both full pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that there was no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5 to 3. The key distinction was between tolerating student speech and promoting it: this newspaper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature as journalism. The Court held that school officials may exercise control over the content they promote. The rights established in Tinker thus acquired their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalls that when she was a kid many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks, and on looking it up finds corporal punishment has still not died out in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's rule specified a paddle under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, in principle one to five swats; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that individual case was excessive but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning: the Eighth Amendment protects the convicted, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by the harsh facts of criminal conviction and imprisonment; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and you can go home after school. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students and students with disabilities struck at significantly higher rates.

33:52 Searching a bag needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 a 14-year-old student known as TLO in New Jersey was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers and kept digging, found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing, and TLO was ultimately convicted and given a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6 to 3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause police require; the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly where they would be; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — sent Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the top.

The person who proposed stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism herself and grounds the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of high information density, with none of the vague communication chicken soup.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and that situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. That worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance in tests, sports or intellectual tasks right there on the spot, and it makes people avoid such situations over the long run, which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety doesn't come from ability — it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media lets labels chase you from every side
Social media's power lies in how fast it spreads sketches of what a group is like, and people have no patience to see the elaboration and the exceptions to such a sketch, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations where "I'll be seen through my identity." It occasionally spreads images that reduce threat too, but the overall tone skews negative, and the result is that in a diverse society, everyone is more alert to their own identity and to what others might be thinking.

6:16 Fifteen minutes of self-reflection can raise grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers simply asked seventh graders to spend 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the chance to let teachers know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise, setting off a positive feedback loop: grades improve → alertness to the label drops → grades improve further. The intervention cost almost nothing, yet it changed long-term trajectories.

9:20 The vigilance of diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people are pulled back and forth between two choices: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility — it's the real pressure the situation imposes; when the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
The experiment had students write an essay about their favorite teacher and then receive critical feedback. The first two ways of giving it — straight criticism, or opening with a "positive halo" — were trusted by white students and deeply distrusted by Black students. The third way added only one line: "We have high standards, because these essays will be published; I read your essay and I believe you can reach them." Under that condition, Black students took their essays home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude thinks the most useful ability is realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust is already there, when in reality people worry about how you see the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are all good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you're human before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power has to send the safety signal first; second, near-obsessive clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm that the person across from them is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connect, be clear, care.

item.title: Latin Doesn't Make Surgeons: A Hard Exam Is Worth Less Than a Useful One
