27:27 Becoming a discovery means passing four gates
If a signal like this arrives again in the future, calling it a true technosignature would require at least four conditions: one, it repeats at the same position, so we know it's still there; two, telescopes at two different locations receive it simultaneously, ruling out Earth interference; three, the signal carries modulation, encoding, or mathematical structure, rather than being a bare carrier; four, known natural processes are ruled out one by one. Historically, when pulsars were first discovered they were nicknamed "little green men," showing that nature can perfectly impersonate intelligence. The right posture isn't to pick a side between belief and mockery, but to allow the excitement and then do everything possible to prove you're fooling yourself.

31:29 Its legacy is a window that was too narrow
The Wow! signal appeared for 72 seconds in exactly the form early SETI hoped to recognize — narrowband, near the hydrogen line, strong enough, shaped like a real source in the sky — and then nothing more was ever heard. It showed what a great discovery might look like before the evidence is sufficient. The host's landing point: the galaxy is 100,000 light-years wide and billions of years old, and even the largest civilization is just one flickering spark within it. If civilizations don't spread, don't transmit often, and don't often point a beam at us, the Fermi paradox may not exist at all. With that 1/1200 of a day, the Wow! signal briefly put that possibility in front of humanity.

item.title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Would Cure the Housing Crisis
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.description: The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to build or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.
item.content:encoded:
The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to build or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.

The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists across the left and right agree on. Lars Doucet turns an abstract tax design into a power struggle, using Houston parking lots, South Korea's appraisal system, and Norway's resource dividends as evidence.

0:05 A land tax is not a property tax, it is a location tax
Lars builds his case on an analogy: the land value tax shares an origin with the ordinary property tax, but it splits ‘building value’ from ‘land value’. A building tax punishes you for constructing, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a good location and letting it sit idle. Land value, he says, comes from the labour of the people around you — your ability to earn a living, go to school, and make friends the moment you walk out the door depends entirely on your neighbours and the whole city. The landlord lies back and sucks that collective value into his own pocket, and that is the paradox of Progress and Poverty: the ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, and land never does.

0:13 The builders are right, but not right enough
The host asks: Oakland relaxed density and rents fell, so do we still need a land tax? Lars concedes that ‘housing shortage’ is the main cause, but points out that YIMBYs never explain one counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet its downtown still holds a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and building together, so the more you build the more tax you pay, while holding and waiting for appreciation is cheaper. Developers therefore have no incentive to develop, only an incentive to lobby for rezoning and then keep holding. Without land tax reform, he says, you end up in a stalemate: ‘you changed the zoning, but I just won't sell.’

0:23 The objections are powered by imagination
Lars sorts the opposition into three camps and takes them apart one by one. How do you appraise land separately from buildings? He says 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something like it: South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels a year and produces nationwide land values in 5 months; Norway trained a national automated valuation model on the state property data platform Finn.no with a core team of just 3 people. Think there will be too many protests? He says the real source of protest is ‘my land looks the same as my neighbour's, so why am I charged more’ — under a land tax, you and your neighbour are assessed on the same location basis, which actually makes it easier. The excuse for not doing it is that nobody has measured it.

0:35 The little old lady is not an argument against it
The sharpest criticism is ‘the transition is unfair’ — on the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalized value of all future tax liability, which amounts to expropriation in one stroke. Lars concedes this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers the guardrail: the move is never a one-step nationwide 100% land tax, but a gradual switchover by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations and most single-family homes actually see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly afraid of being driven out of the old family home, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: you owe it, and it is deducted with interest from the estate after death.

0:41 Britain's failure was a capacity problem
The most commonly cited counterexample online is Britain's 1910s ‘People's Budget’: the valuation took 6 years and was overturned by shopkeepers' protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: the much-shared article is simply ‘deriving a universal law from one sample’, and it simultaneously claims that ‘a pure land tax has never succeeded’ and that ‘land cannot be valued’ — even though South Korea has been appraising nationwide land values parcel by parcel for decades. That only proves the British state machine was weak, he says, not that a land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, instead of passing off lazy ignorance as a verdict.

0:45 Norway achieved Georgism through resource dividends
Lars points to a fact that makes Norway a ‘success story’ today: the entire Norwegian resource management regime is Georgist in structure — natural resources such as oil are treated as the property of all the people, and extractors pay extremely high resource taxes, while production and investment themselves are not punished, so entrepreneurship is encouraged and the natural bounty flows into the treasury to fund universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except that it is not on land value. This ‘Norwegian paradox’ leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state, it can be its foundation.

0:51 The automobile opened a second frontier
Lars explains why the land question that gripped every city 100 years ago later vanished: the frontier is itself a mechanism of ‘free land’ — as long as you can still expand into the wilderness, the poor do not have to face the squeeze of ‘high wages plus high rent’. America's first frontier was westward expansion, and when it closed Henry George appeared; in the 20th century the automobile turned the suburbs into a ‘second frontier’ that lasted another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006-2008. He says people now call this a ‘second Gilded Age’, but it is just a script from over a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work, as a ‘third frontier’, held out for roughly 5 minutes before capital digested it.

0:53 Don't win online, do the politicians' homework
The closing answer is very practical: Lars says the most effective way to create change he has learned in the past 5 years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but taking every objection a state senator or city council member might raise, running the data simulations and preparing the answers in advance, and putting them directly on their desks — ‘doing politicians' homework’, he says, is an absurd but extraordinarily effective strategy. Several states have already passed bills allowing land tax reform. His call to action: go measure, don't guess.

item.title: What Drives Founders Isn't Becoming a Billionaire, It's the Fear of the Server Crashing at 3 A.M.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/
item.description: Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is the fear of disaster — the server going down, the model train about to fall off the table; keep your head down for ten years, look up and do the math, and you discover you're already a billionaire at the last round's valuation.
item.content:encoded:
Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is the fear of disaster — the server going down, the model train about to fall off the table; keep your head down for ten years, look up and do the math, and you discover you're already a billionaire at the last round's valuation.

After 21 years and 47 batches, PG's judgment: AI has changed almost nothing about startups, only the bill. Useful for calibrating your confidence in "this time is different."

2:02 People nostalgic for the golden age forget that all it had was Reddit
Since roughly 2008 people have been saying YC is finished — PG's read is that its attackers have to first admit it was once great, so all they can ever say is "not what it used to be." But his counterexample is concrete: the flagship of the supposed good old days was Reddit, whereas the project he did office hours with this episode was intercontinental ballistic freight — like an ICBM, except it doesn't explode on landing, it unloads. Another category was curing cancer. He says there are too many ways to go at it — a vaccine at one end, therapies at the other — so you should fund several, and any one that works is worth it. This episode had a company doing on-demand research for cancer patients, and what he liked was exactly that approach: cancer is famously not solved by "coming up with a cure," and maybe the way to beat it is death by a thousand cuts.

4:09 Google won't be breached, it will be obsoleted by the world
Many of the ideas in the 2012 "frighteningly ambitious" list have already been done, and one of them was "the new Google." PG says he predicted the path back then: you can't attack Google head-on, you can only wait for the day the world changes enough that its model goes stale. OpenAI is that change itself — after using it he found he no longer used search, because what he wanted was never web pages, it was information, so he just asks the AI. It's a corollary that holds for every incumbent: a moat isn't breached, it's obsoleted.

6:15 Ambition is the ticket in; the daily fuel is fear of looking like a fool
Ambition is a necessity, because the obstacles in a startup are too terrifying to push through on conscientiousness alone. But PG says what actually gets a founder moving at any given moment isn't "if I solve this I'll become a billionaire," it's the fear of disaster: the server going down, the fear of looking like an idiot. His image is a toy train — the engine is going over the edge of the table and you lunge to catch it. You keep your head down fixing that train for ten years, look up and do the math on the last round's valuation, and discover you're already a billionaire. He says sometimes he's the one who does the math first and tells the founder.

9:21 The only test of formidable is whether they get what they want
Formidable is a private word PG and Jessica were using before YC. His definition is operational: this person gets what they want in any situation — if they don't, what does formidable even mean. That definition incidentally explains the investing logic: you hold stock in his company, he holds it too, interests are aligned; he gets what he wants, you get what you want. It's also the precondition for his answer to "where does the next trillion-dollar company come from."

11:24 Lean startup isn't dead: even rocket companies can start small
Asked whether lean startup is dead and whether you now have to burn big money from day one, PG's rebuttal has two layers. First, price: tokens are expensive now only because of the GPU shortage, and the price for the same level of inference will fall by roughly 30x a year, and on top of that you're getting higher-quality tokens — technology always gets cheaper. Second, path: even rocket companies can start with modest money; you can't build a real rocket, but you can produce a design, run simulations, show it to experts, and if it's convincing enough you get the next round. StarCloud wrote a white paper and booked a launch — though he adds that that founder was himself a well-known expert in the field with built-in credibility, and a fresh graduate doesn't have it that easy.

13:24 AI went the wrong direction: from human toward perfect
People doing AI in the 1980s thought the path started from "the perfect fly": able to do only what a fly does, but as well as a fly does it; then climb up to mouse, cat, monkey, human, each level perfect. What we got was the reverse — a complete human right out of the gate, just talking nonsense, like an undergrad trying to bluff his way through a paper. The dimension being optimized was the opposite one: not from perfect toward human, but from human toward perfect. That also explains the jagged frontier: it can solve hard math problems but can't tell you what time a restaurant opens.

16:30 AI changes the bill structure, not the shipping speed
PG says the metric that still best predicts startup success is shipping speed, and AI hasn't replaced that metric — with these tools in hand, plenty of companies this episode still weren't shipping fast enough, which shows the difference isn't how fast you can write things, you first have to come up with the ideas. "With AI, what hasn't changed?" His answer: so far almost everything is exactly the same. The only strange new thing is the bill structure — the biggest cost of a startup used to be salaries, everything else was cheap by comparison; now there's GPU on top, and tokens can burn tens of thousands of dollars a day.

19:36 The next trillion-dollar company comes from the right person, not the right idea
Asked where the next trillion-dollar company will come from, PG swaps the question from sector to person: it comes from the right founder, not some particular idea — startup ideas are highly variable, and the most he'll say is "probably not dog-walking." Conversely, to judge whether a company is worth investing in, first judge whether the founder is formidable, and what they're doing is probably promising. As for whether future founders will look different, he says there's already 20 years of data, today's founders are exactly the same as 20 years ago, and there's no reason the next 20 years will be different.

item.title: Arm Moves Into Making CPUs: The Biggest Bottleneck in Chip Design Is Verification, Not Design
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.description: The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.
item.content:encoded:
The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.

It uses real internal Arm data to explain what AI is actually good for in chip design, then ties product, capital and supply-chain judgments into one closed loop — worth checking against your own expectations if you work in AI infrastructure.

3:43 Arm is building CPUs itself because customers are pushing it to
Arm used to sell only IP licenses at 98.5% gross margin, never touching inventory or wafers. One step forward, the compute subsystem already had customers grabbing pre-assembled CPU, GPU and memory "subsystems" as modules. The next step came because "customers who want a general-purpose CPU for the large-model era can't find a supplier" and went straight to Arm to push for one. Before announcing, Arm asked nearly every license customer, and there was very little opposition: a bigger software ecosystem benefits every customer, so Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft and Google — all companies making Arm server chips — publicly supported it.

8:07 Banning AI tools is sending engineers back to the library
The total chip design cycle is 24-36 months; the biggest time sink is not RTL generation or architecture mapping, but verification, validation, debug and documentation. AI is especially well suited to these steps, and roughly 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily. Turning the tools off is like telling people in the 1990s they could only use the internet two hours a day and had to go back downstairs to the library for the rest. Where AI is currently weakest is RTL generation and physical design, because models depend on public corpora while the industry's most critical details are private data — exactly the gap companies like Arm can fill.

10:35 From idea to layout is five years away, not two or three
The host asked: once AI eats verification, the most time-consuming step, can 24-36 months shrink to 6-12 months? Rene Haas gave a measured answer: 2-3 years is unrealistic; five years or more, for designs with not-too-complex constraints, going from an idea all the way to GDSII (the layout file handed to the fab) is possible. If you type into the tool "make a chip 10% faster, 20% cheaper and 30% more power-efficient than some reference," don't expect one-click completion. His judgment is that in 5-10 years the whole industry's design methodology will change noticeably.

15:00 AI supply and demand are still far apart, and the bottleneck is the construction site, not the wafer
On the AI bubble, Rene Haas argues you have to separate valuation froth at the stock level from the industry chain itself; he says plainly that supply versus demand is still "far apart." Transformer inference and training eat both compute and memory, and demand won't stop. The real hard constraint will move to data center construction: many projects are running late and need more workers, and in various places resistance to new data center builds is emerging; over the next 3-5 years the constraint may not be wafer capacity or memory, but the physical construction step staying perpetually tight.

17:14 SoftBank doing cloud is about being a customer for chip companies
For capital-heavy, capex-intensive chip/AI founders: access to capital is itself the gate, and strategic partnerships need to reach early into three layers — supply chain, PE and banks. Behind Arm is SoftBank, and not just as a shareholder; SoftBank just announced it will build a "neo cloud"-style cloud service, which lets young chip companies avoid only knocking on Microsoft's or Google's door for a design win and instead form a direct customer relationship with the Arm/SoftBank ecosystem — one more path to deployment.

21:25 Humanoids won't unify everything; specialized robots will coexist long-term
Rene Haas sees robot 1.0 as purpose-built: both mechanics and software optimized for a single motion, so switching a production line means nearly starting over. A new generation of robots that can redefine tasks through training and have a general-purpose mechanical body will first take over repetitive labor in construction, infrastructure and security. Form factor won't go in a single direction: factories, warehouses and tools are all designed to human dimensions, so humanoids have an advantage; another set of tasks is better served by specialized forms. Cost has to come down first, and delivery and warehousing will be the earliest scenarios to automate.

27:13 Restricting chips to China is an unwinnable infinite game
On US manufacturing he is direct: the US should build more fabs at home, needed both for national security and for supply-chain diversification. On export controls, he frames it as an "infinite game" — restricting chips to China cannot produce a victory with an end state, and may instead push key technology out of the US. He also rejects the idea that data centers are "big warehouses with no jobs": energy, liquid cooling and the surrounding ecosystem are all jobs that can be created in the US.

36:00 In a token world, every path goes through a CPU
If you use the token factory metaphor for accelerators, Rene Haas thinks the real system question is: who orchestrates and arbitrates where those tokens go, and delivers them to users. He believes every path goes through a CPU: beyond training, there's inference scheduling, system orchestration, context and tool calls. At the edge, on devices that can't fit a 50W GPU, Arm's power advantage is even more obvious. The CPU hasn't disappeared — it's forming persistent demand alongside accelerators.

item.title: The Number One Fraud Red Flag Isn't Greed — It's Personal Finances Already Out of Control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.description: For 14 straight years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a shut-down critical brain region, and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.
item.content:encoded:
For 14 straight years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a shut-down critical brain region, and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.

One author is a clinical neuropsychologist, the other has 20 years of experience suing financial advisers; the offender profiles and warning signals here have more screening value than moral slogans.

2:04 The only test for crossing the line: "This is not your money"
Moira defines financial misconduct as "doing bad things with other people's money": it includes both taking money for yourself and guiding or advising others to use funds in ways that aren't in their best interest. She stresses that anyone working in finance must always remember "this is not your money." Reducing the ethical question to fiduciary duty gives all the later warning signals a single baseline for judgment.

9:10 The top red flag for 14 straight years is personal financial problems
Philippa cites ACFE's global report: for 14 consecutive years, the number one fraud red flag hasn't been greed but "personal financial problems" — people whose personal finances are out of control, who can't make ends meet, or who are drowning in debt are the most likely to get involved in financial misconduct. The financial industry offers access to other people's money and attracts people who chase wealth, and on top of that people are irrational about money; these three conditions stack into fertile ground for misconduct.

13:14 Listening to advice, the brain is like it's praying: the critical region goes offline
Moira notes that neuroimaging evidence shows that when people receive financial advice, key critical regions of the brain go "offline," in a state similar to the brain during prayer. People feel safe, trusting, and open, and this non-critical state heightens vulnerability, especially for those unfamiliar with finance. She gives the example that even hedge fund managers will "sit and wait for answers" in front of an adviser rather than asking how a product actually works.

19:19 Good people start erring through obedience and eagerness, not greed
Philippa and Moira break down the path by which good people go wrong: blindly obeying orders, crossing lines out of "misguided helpfulness," then hiding the mistake out of fear, then covering it with a bigger lie. The book's "John" slides from a small slip into lying, then into doubling down on the cover-up. Moira stresses that ethics isn't a solo sport but a team sport; if the organizational culture tacitly permits misconduct, it's very hard for an individual to stay clean alone.

37:36 Psychopaths flow into finance disproportionately
Responding to Cameron's concern, Moira says the evidence shows psychopaths flow disproportionately into finance and business because "that's where the money is." She cites Robert Hare's research: successful psychopaths tend to be charming and extremely good at sensing and exploiting other people's desires. The damage they do is large, and they often keep moving within the industry because colleagues feel "relief" when they leave, leaving the problem for the next firm.

53:50 Most people don't realize they're making an ethical decision at all
Traditional ethics training always presents clear moral dilemmas in a classroom, but real-world problems tend to arise quietly, so people don't realize they're at a fork in the road. Moira cites Kahneman's "what you see is all there is": people don't proactively question the motives of product providers, don't think about who benefits from a complex product, and won't admit they don't actually understand it. The result is that even with ethics training, most of the time they have no idea they're facing a moral decision.

1:02:56 The future wrongdoer is a vulnerable ordinary person, not a bad guy
Philippa lists the profile of the future wrongdoer: early in their career (Evan got pulled into a global fraud one month after joining and was banned for life nine months later), in debt, highly dependent on their boss, people-pleasing, low self-esteem (compensated for with a luxury car), fatigued, family problems, and so on. These signals are rarely used by the industry to screen advisers for their own biases; they aren't some rare evil but the common weaknesses of ordinary people under pressure and vulnerability.

1:09:07 20 years of suing, never once sued a CFP holder
Philippa practiced law for 20 years and sued many financial professionals, but never once sued any CFP holder. She believes there's no simple way to pick out a good adviser, but having a certification is a positive signal. She also offers a test: if an adviser only talks about investments and doesn't understand the client's whole life situation, that's just wealth management, not financial planning — the subject of planning is the person, not the assets.

item.title: The 5% Treasury Yield Isn't About Inflation: $32 Trillion of Debt Means Buyers Will Only Take More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.description: Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply every year, and Treasury buybacks can't hold it down.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply every year, and Treasury buybacks can't hold it down.

The mainstream narrative pins the 30-year at 5% on inflation; this episode offers a genuinely additive alternative framework, folding the limits of Treasury intervention, the mechanics of Fed balance-sheet runoff, and the term premium debate into one logic.

4:04 5% is first a Treasury interest bill, not a macro signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5% — even after it ticked down slightly that day following the Fed chair's remarks. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but Treasury's predicament: if I were the Treasury secretary, what I'd see is that US government interest expense is extraordinarily high, and I'd have to find a way to push yields down. That line sets the frame for the whole episode: the official side has a strong incentive to push long-end rates down, but whether it can and whether it should are the premises for everything that follows.

5:07 Treasury wants to sell another $10 billion, it can only pay more
Daryl gives the episode's central thought experiment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund that already holds $20 billion of 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion — why won't you? The answer: at a 5.3% yield you've already made the allocation you want, and to get you to add, you'd have to be paid a higher interest rate as compensation. The logic incidentally explains the structural shift on the demand side — foreign central banks are already full up and no longer buying, so new Treasury supply has to land on domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, hedge funds, and that money is highly sensitive to yield.

8:10 The logic didn't change; the debt stock hit a tipping point
Joe raises the objection that has to be faced: aging populations, a political system with no appetite for spending cuts, unsustainable deficits — that bearish logic existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was talked about that way for decades, so why did yields keep falling then and why are they rising now? Daryl's answer is a scale effect: the 60% debt/GDP red line the IMF drew back then is far behind us, France is already at 100%; the US Treasury market has grown from about $18 trillion to $31 trillion, and keeps expanding. There's no new logic — the quantity of debt itself has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The long end's 5% is mostly issuance, not inflation expectations
Since the short end is still held down by high inflation and the Fed, why not attribute the high 30-year yield directly to inflation expectations? Daryl concedes inflation over the past five years has indeed been well above the Fed's target and the job isn't done, but points out: implied inflation expectations backed out of real versus nominal bonds aren't flashing alarm; the investors actually buying and selling 10-, 20-, and 30-year Treasuries aren't processing inflation first in their heads — they're processing supply relative to demand. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework — right now the main driver of the term premium is issuance, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to cap yields are just a signal, with far too little ammunition
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, with liquidity as the official rationale. Daryl reads the subtext directly: from the wording of his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity — he thinks yields are ‘too high’, and he says outright that he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the size of Treasury's operations is a drop in the bucket relative to the whole Treasury market, and the market moved briefly on the news then reversed fast. Trying to use the government's own resources to suppress the path of yields has a precedent in the 1992 sterling crisis — and Bessent was the man at Soros's fund who shorted the pound.

19:22 Buybacks' real job is sweeping up old bonds, not managing rates
The original design of the buyback program wasn't rate management: as Treasury keeps issuing new securities, a lot of illiquid off-the-run old bonds pile up in the market, clogging dealer balance sheets and trading away from a smooth yield curve. A paper Daryl is working on with two New York Fed economists tests whether sweeping up the fragments on a ‘regular, predictable’ schedule and swapping in new issues can improve market liquidity and earn taxpayers a buy-low, sell-high return. The phrase ‘odd lots’ is in fact where the show's name comes from. He thinks that kind of routine operation works; Treasury stepping in at a moment of emergency to defend its own bond market is a different matter.

25:30 The runoff constraint is reserves, not the asset side
A new Fed chair wants to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only stare at the asset side. Daryl points to the arithmetic constraint: selling assets requires extinguishing an equal amount of liabilities. Of the three liability buckets, the TGA can't have Treasury pull its deposits out, and circulating cash can't be recalled, so the only compressible item is commercial banks' reserves at the Fed. But today reserves are ‘the Swiss Army knife of the financial industry’: they pay interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are usable for payments at any time, so banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect Acharya and Rajan described at Jackson Hole in 2017 already made the point: every time the Fed expands its balance sheet, banks get addicted to reserves, and shrinking it necessarily causes market volatility.

28:33 The task force will swap duration, not actually shrink the size
Daryl states he has no inside information on the task force, but makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem isn't size but composition, and the sensible move is to gradually replace the Fed's long-dated Treasuries with short-term bills, so that reserve interest expense on the liability side offsets bill interest income on the asset side in the same direction, reducing the hit to the Fed's own P&L from policy-rate swings; second, don't keep mortgage-backed securities on the asset side — let them roll off naturally. His own conclusion is blunter: the Fed doesn't necessarily have to shrink the balance sheet, but it must have the tools in hand to shrink it on its own, or it will be backed into a corner when Congress applies pressure.

item.title: A wallet's profit engine isn't float interest — it's money moving inside the system
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.description: The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and cash-out charges again. It earns the spread on movement, not interest on balances — and PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on that model.
item.content:encoded:
The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and cash-out charges again. It earns the spread on movement, not interest on balances — and PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on that model.

It takes the wallet cost structure apart for real: wholesale network pricing under ten cents, while platforms can charge users several times that; Japanese players even open multiple bank accounts to route around clearing. Useful as a business teardown even if you don't do payments.

1:05 A wallet has to answer how it makes money on day one
It opens with the author's own $100 Venmo bill to a barber: for a small transaction that already has a mature payment rail, why does PayPal still want to wedge itself in and monetize it. Then it quickly sets the scope: this is about the e-wallet business, not crypto private-key wallets; because it looks like it can hold and disburse balances, it immediately enters the regulatory zone that treats deposits as sensitive, so a wallet has to answer how it makes money from the first day of design — fail that, and the product dies.

5:14 Card fraud isn't scammers building sites, it's issuer-side leaks
The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was that users didn't dare hand over their card numbers, and the media kept amplifying carding risk. The author points out the facts are the opposite: most fraud comes from massive data leaks on the issuer side, not from fraudsters parasitizing checkout pages, and concludes that "economies of scale protect criminals too." PayPal's value was standing between the user and the card number and the recipient, capping the risk of a single transaction — which gave it grounds to charge a toll near 3%, and planted the seed for the balance design that followed.

6:19 A free wallet is not free at all for the wallet itself
Putting money into a wallet goes through the card networks, at a historical list price of about 3%, and the wallet eats that cost; but once the balance stays inside the system, transfers between users amount to changing a row in a database, too cheap to bill for. PayPal charges close to full price on both the in and out ends, so simply substituting internal transfers for external ones adds a slice of gross margin. A wallet that is free to the average user is not free to the wallet — the zero marginal cost of the float is the real dam.

9:21 Driving down network fees beats product innovation for profit
There is no necessary relationship between wholesale and retail: buying millions of ACH transactions costs about $0.05 each, while a payment processor can quote merchants close to $0.30; the spread is the tax the platform levies on the underlying plumbing. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about 200 yen per transaction while intra-bank entries are nearly free, so some products open accounts at each of the top banks, move the user's money inside the banks, and settle via daily netting. In finance, driving down network fees converts into wallet profit more directly than product innovation does.

12:27 Cash-out isn't a user perk, it's a second toll pipe
Cash App prices cash-out the same way: want it fast, pick the pricier card rail, charged at 1.75% with a 25-cent minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted 88 cents. Paired with that is issuing prepaid cards through partners like Sutton Bank, so money spent outside the system still captures swipe fees. The wallet no longer treats cash-out as a user benefit but as a second revenue pipe, because the partner bank needs the wallet's user scale and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

20:53 On co-brand cards the wallet takes a cut and carries the defaults
The logic of a wallet co-branding a credit card is charging on both sides, but risk control is the real battlefield: wallets typically assume their accumulated spending data lets them underwrite more accurately than the issuing bank. The industry has repeatedly shown FICO is already strong enough to be hard to replace; the extra variables that could meaningfully improve losses tend to cross legal red lines. What actually prices the wallet is the agreement — the bank requires the whole loan portfolio's loss rate to stay under a threshold, or the wallet's revenue share goes to zero or even turns negative. The 10-K language dances around "loss sharing," but in essence the wallet is carrying the issuer's bad debt.

24:50 Users care about the phone, not the plastic card
Apple's core argument when negotiating with banks is that users care about the phone, not the plastic credit card; if the bank won't pay, Apple can also back or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. The reported figure is that Apple takes 15 basis points per Apple Pay transaction, while Google reportedly takes nothing — which the author uses to needle the two giants' differing ability to do non-core products. The next layer is the conclusion that the checkout counter itself can work like ad inventory: once the goods and prices are fixed, who gets their payment method ranked first becomes a bidding war, and Stripe has already turned the traditional display into dynamic ordering by user preference, even opening up merchant fine-tuning options.

31:13 Network fees don't fall at the negotiating table, they fall in the default setting
Extend Link into a general-ledger-level settlement negotiation layer: if users store their low-cost payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass the card networks and go through bank accounts; the network fees saved get redistributed between merchants and users. This can't be negotiated by one company sitting at one table — it's the aggregation of decisions by millions of users and merchants, ultimately representing a side of the payments negotiating table with volume approaching 1% of global GDP. Only that total has the standing to reprice network fees.

item.title: If It Can't Solve Quantum Gravity, It Isn't Real AGI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.description: A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is what counts. The conversation also makes clear the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — once searched-for materials have to pass the synthesizability gate, you may be left with zero.
item.content:encoded:
A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is what counts. The conversation also makes clear the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — once searched-for materials have to pass the synthesizability gate, you may be left with zero.

A noise-cancelling pass on the AI world's default judgments: a string theorist makes the returns from science and the boundaries of AI concrete and verifiable, useful for calibrating your own time expectations in hard tech. The narrative is a bit slow, with the substance concentrated in the middle and later sections.

17:28 Learning too much paralyzes you; only naivety dares ask the original questions
The hardest part of going from student to researcher isn't absorbing knowledge, it's posing the original questions that push the boundary of knowledge forward. Gopakumar describes this transition as ‘naivety plus experience’: learn too much and you get paralyzed, so you need to keep a bit of naivety to dare ask the questions that look impossible to get a handle on; a mentor's job is to teach you to break a big problem into small steps you can advance right now, without losing sight of the ultimate goal. His own advisor David Gross was very good at this — by his account, Gross's first student did the work that won the two of them a Nobel Prize, and Witten also won a Fields Medal. Now he trains his students by replicating the same method: the first one or two problems are assigned by him, and even he doesn't have the answers, and he works alongside the student slowly through their third or fourth year, after which they ask their own questions independently.

28:36 Spacetime isn't a background, it's an emergent approximation
Think of string theory the way you think of water being made of discrete atoms: the continuous spacetime we touch is most likely just a low-resolution approximation of some deeper structure at macroscopic scales. Gopakumar stresses this isn't pure speculation — quantum mechanics itself doesn't allow spacetime to be treated as an infinitely divisible smooth background; add black holes (Hawking and others found they have many anomalous properties) and the breakdown of the Big Bang at the singularity, and physicists have to answer ‘where does spacetime come from’. String theory happens to provide a natural framework: spacetime emerges from something more fundamental, and gravity and the known interactions fit inside it too. This explains why he treats ‘solving quantum gravity’ as a very high bar for intelligence: it demands not just the ability to solve problems, but the construction of new conceptual frameworks.

39:45 Materials should be designed in reverse: fix the property, then find the structure
Start with a long-horizon yardstick: quantum mechanics was originally just about understanding the atom, and the devices it now underpins account, by his estimate, for roughly 35%-40% of US GDP, while the commercial ripples only became obvious four or five decades after the theory appeared. He calls the current phase the second quantum revolution: quantum materials like graphene, discovered by accident, are already commercializing, and the next step is inverse materials design with AI — first define what properties a material needs, then search for what structure can deliver them and how to synthesize it, bypassing traditional trial-and-error chemistry. He also reveals a conversation with Demis Hassabis: DeepMind's next holy grail is finding a room-temperature superconductor, and Hassabis told him from the start not to talk about quantum gravity.

50:59 Being stuck is the norm; keep three or four problems in the air at once
Being stuck isn't the exception, it's a researcher's daily life; especially during the student-to-researcher transition, being stuck can feel like a crush (being overwhelmed). Gopakumar's first strategy is portfolio hedging: push three or four problems at once, and when one dies, switch to another — probabilistically, one of them will move half a step. The second move is to go teach — the moment a student's eyes light up, that satisfaction can pull you out of a trough, and he has repeatedly found that ‘after a lecture, a stuck problem suddenly opens up’. The third move is to deliberately learn something new you've always wanted to learn but never had time for, to switch to a new frame of reference before returning to the old problem.

55:08 Talent is multiplicative, not additive; the shortage is never headcount
Why does top-tier science cluster in a few places rather than spreading evenly? Gopakumar gives the mechanism: talking in the same place, using each other as sounding boards, keeps the brain in a constantly stimulated state even without formal collaboration; and once real collaboration happens, the different skills two people bring multiply rather than add. He borrows a physics metaphor: photons in an ordinary light bulb are chaotic, photons in a laser are coherent with one another, and a group of people that achieves coherence will also produce a lasing effect like a laser. He says many Indian institutions actually underperform relative to their talent, and what's missing isn't headcount but this resonant atmosphere; that's why ICTS's founding principle is simple — hire only first-rate people, give them resources and freedom, and don't let them lower their ambitions.

1:11:19 AI can accelerate research, but it can't make conceptual leaps
AI just won two Nobel Prizes in a row, but Gopakumar splits ‘AI for science’ and ‘science for AI’ into two separate things: the former he grants is an overdrive gear, with AI accelerating a certain very narrow class of tasks in research; but the ‘theory’ AI does today is still far from his conceptual-layer standard, and the best physics relies on conceptual leaps rather than pattern recognition. Conversely, he's more bullish on science for AI — among the people who discovered scaling laws at Anthropic are those with physics backgrounds; Hopfield was himself a statistical physicist, using simple physical models to simulate the brain. Along this path, physicists might join computer scientists and neuroscientists to take AI from language models to physics-inspired world models. This distinction is worth remembering.

1:21:32 After the synthesizability gate, zero new AI materials are left
The soberest bucket of cold water in the whole session came from the audience Q&A: Google claims to have discovered a large number of new materials with AI, but after filtering out feasibility and the synthesizability gate, Gopakumar's phrasing is ‘I think left with zero’ — zero left. His stance isn't to deny AI materials science (someone in the same session cited Microsoft's DFT model with only 385,000 parameters that bypasses traditional hybrid methods), but to remind you the whole chain is still long: after predicting a crystal structure you still have to grow it and scale it, and every step can filter out the surprises. He says India should also bet along this chain. That line is a useful reverse calibration for the ‘AI discovers new materials’ narrative.

item.title: AI's Front-Runners Are Just Refineries, Not the Native-App Winners
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.description: AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are only refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.
item.content:encoded:
AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are only refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.

Zeng Ming uses a three-stage industrial history to give you a coordinate system for where AI stands — an antidote to the optimism of "this time is different," plus the window of opportunity for application founders and a brutal forecast for incumbents' transformation.

16:28 Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of a general-purpose technology into three stages: first it becomes social infrastructure, then applications explode, and finally native applications appear. In 2026, token as a unit of measure reaching consensus shows the first stage has matured; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called "lobster") mark AI's formal entry into the agent stage. He draws the analogy to the 1992 website-building movement: back then people built websites to share information, today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet, and whoever can establish the agent standard and seize the user entry point may hold the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

27:49 A ten-trillion-dollar company will appear, but not these two
Zeng Ming says plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technological and commercial achievements, but business history shows the first wave of breakout companies is most likely not the big winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, AOL was valued at $220 billion, and neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that refine the base oil — the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly exist in the future, but not necessarily the two currently in the lead. Model companies will move toward a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

1:10:29 The unit of an AI-native organization is the task, not the job
The company corresponds to the industrial age's bureaucracy; AI overturns the industrial age, and the corporate system will wither. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not the job but the task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around "what needs to be solved," with humans and AI coordinating around tasks. So well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, and the traditional middle layer will die out too; future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form, and OpenAI itself is more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of the new organization is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing and co-creation, no longer relying on commands and performance reviews.

1:31:32 Excellence can only be judged in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
Zeng Ming argues that "good ≠ great." Being good is growth that keeps receiving positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming negative feedback again and again, persisting when everyone disapproves, and finally proving through enormous success that you were the era's prophet — which is why "greatness is judged in hindsight." Good people easily fall into a loop of proving themselves, which makes their strategies conservative. Great people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the times and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders he asks, "Ten years from now, what kind of self would you be satisfied with?" If the answer is "a ten-billion-dollar company," that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly great founders tend to be altruistic and empathetic.

1:47:24 Strategy in the AI era can't be planned, only generated
In the AI era strategy is not planned but generated. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": the organization must build an environment and network in which strategic insight emerges naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are higher, a CEO cannot plan by linear extrapolation, nor outsource strategy to McKinsey — McKinsey's explosion was a product of the industrial age's slow maturation. His methodology is "look ten years out, think three years out, act one year out," with the core being "think three years out": you must at least see two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term action and the mid-term picture. Organization-building must guarantee enough context rather than control, letting the right people make the right decisions at the right time.

2:01:39 The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
Zeng Ming believes robotics is still in a strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. The current two paths — build a generalized brain first or close the scenario loop first — are both logically valid, and no one can judge in advance which is faster. By historical analogy, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and only entered scale when Ford built the assembly line in 1913; robots have yet to reach their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But the better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented came countless categories — refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners — and robots interacting with the physical world will have N kinds of big scenarios, with home, companionship and industrial uses each potentially producing their own native giants.

2:03:39 The incumbents who feel safe are the least safe
Zeng Ming says that before a giant wave no one is safe, and feeling safe is the most unsafe thing of all. In business history no era's companies have ever transitioned smoothly into the next era; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that overturns the industrial revolution, not a continuity innovation like mobile internet, so old giants' technical reserves and organizational culture are negative assets. Google can live on as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is likewise not naturally safe. The new platform will most likely be created by a new company.

2:20:56 Human value lies in conjuring from nothing, not writing songs or painting
Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI, and people are on one hand forced and on the other finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is called creativity — not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and conjure something from nothing. AI has already taken away all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. That is why he calls his own mission "to be a happy researcher," and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, with even the education system forced to shift from "knowledge instillation" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

item.title: The Moat in AI Writing Isn't the Model — It's the Proprietary Data You Feed It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.description: Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. Her core method isn't prompt tricks — it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. Her core method isn't prompt tricks — it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.

Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer turned AI into a mode of production. The meat is in the last 30 minutes; the earlier personal story provides the motivational backdrop.

2:09 An AI coach's biggest value isn't saving money
After being laid off, she was in a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20/month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing out her thoughts and letting AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalize thinking, counter catastrophizing, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of this experience wasn't the money saved — it was the belief that AI could actually drive concrete change in her life. At the time she was hesitating about accepting Every's freelance offer; ChatGPT gave her a nudge to just try it.

8:26 Output comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
She once delivered 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts, and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do that not because she wrote smarter one-line prompts, but because she did extensive upfront context engineering: feeding brand info, product details, audience profiles, and differentiators to the model in one go. Much of the demand was essentially content reuse, and AI is good at rewriting a long article into versions for different platforms. Her rule: set up the scene early, and the rest runs fast.

11:28 Give the model a fence before talking tone and word choice
Before Claude Projects existed, she had to keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into the context each time. This structure didn't come out of nowhere — it's the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what their pain points are, how the product addresses them, who the competitors are, and where the differences lie. She says this gives the model a fenced playground, ensuring it won't go off track before you talk about word choice, tone, and reading level. When Projects launched, she set up a separate project for each client and each column.

15:40 The last mile of AI writing can only be filled by humans
She believes there's a 'last mile problem' in AI writing: models have knowledge cutoffs and aren't in the real physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw 'write a blog post about style guides' at the model, you'll get generic content it already knows — commoditized information. What makes writing unique is fresh ingredients the model hasn't seen: internal company research, third-party reports, personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human provides the good ingredients.

22:50 AI's value is reducing friction, not just speeding up output
She speaks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster — it's reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care physician for three years, then had Codex find a doctor who accepted her insurance and new patients, and complete the appointment. Email is pre-filtered by automation, and only messages that truly need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't using AI as a production tool but as supportive technology that makes her daily functioning 'as a person' easier.

27:03 Let AI interview you repeatedly, and it can prioritize for you
Two years ago she simply asked ChatGPT 'can you be my career coach'; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her job profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a reader praise folder, and OKRs. She doesn't maintain a dashboard herself; she uses voice conversations to have the system prioritize by highest impact, and the system maintains the Kanban for her. The key to building this system was letting AI interview her repeatedly, then distilling those conversations into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

32:27 Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
The core of the Compound Writing plugin is a compounding mindset: every piece of feedback you give AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and adapted it for writing: code and writing both have stages like brainstorming, planning, drafting, and review, except writing focuses more on structure, voice, and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that handles sentence by sentence, and a final pass for publication checks. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window; she feeds fresh daily material into this system.

39:19 Vonnegut as editor gives perspective, not verdicts
She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's suspense principle about the bomb under the table, and Sorkin's and Sedaris's expression styles into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether the story starts as close to the end as possible and whether every sentence earns its place; Hitchcock's lens asks whether the reader will want to keep reading. She stresses this isn't about having the master's soul grade your draft — it's giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject. Non-professional writers might benefit even more because they're less likely to nitpick themselves while writing.

item.title: The stronger the model, the more lethal dirty data: cleaning becomes more valuable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.description: Jane Street's alt data team finds: once data leaks future information into the past, stronger models become more dangerous; nailing down 'what was known at the time' is worth more than tuning the model.
item.content:encoded:
Jane Street's alt data team finds: once data leaks future information into the past, stronger models become more dangerous; nailing down 'what was known at the time' is worth more than tuning the model.

This episode is dense with how data engineering actually creates value; the latter half on correcting data, timestamps, and cost models offers judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.

2:06 Patterns get competed away once discovered
Eric defines this as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, patterns you find are often quickly digested by others and the market, then stop working; knowledge that can accumulate long-term like physical laws is rare. Because of this, the signal-to-noise ratio in trading data is naturally poor—the whole market mechanism is to squeeze out extractable signals, leaving what's closer to a random walk. To keep winning, you must constantly seek new facts, not cling to old patterns.

19:21 Prices can go negative; don't hardcode assumptions into systems
On April 20, 2020, CME crude futures near expiry settled at a negative price—just that one day, and the final settlement later turned positive. The reason wasn't that oil had no value, but that storage at the delivery point, Cushing, was nearly full and no one wanted to take physical delivery. Systems for order entry and risk that long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some couldn't place orders, others didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion: a large part of trading is understanding the messy details of reality—storage capacity, contract multipliers, quote units. When systems get these details right, risk limits can be properly drawn.

32:33 Domain experts don't know how good tools can be
For data and systems to be truly usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have high tolerance for painful processes, worn down by Excel and manual workflows to the point they don't know they deserve better tools; conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the real mechanics of the domain to engineers, and 'how good it can get' to traders. At Jane Street, every desk now has such an embedded developer, a role that grew out of this need.

59:04 Parking spot counts don't equal sales
A classic alt data example is counting cars in Walmart parking lots—more people in cars means better business. Eric says this example is actually bad: what you want to infer is spending, and parking spots only tell you foot traffic, quite indirect; about 20% of Walmart's shopping happens online, and cities like New York have no lots to count. More direct signals are on the transaction side: issuing banks, Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit union processing systems know how much people actually spend, and can sell anonymized aggregate statistics to buy-side firms.

1:04:08 Corrected data turns backtests into time machines
When deciding whether to subscribe to a data feed, the vendor may have already corrected past errors; backtesting on pretty corrected data tests not what you would have actually received at the time, but the correct answers known only later. Eric says that's like simulating having a time machine. Jane Street's solution: save every raw piece of data and the local timestamp of when it was received, so no matter how many transformations you do later, you can reconstruct 'what we knew at that moment.' This is the same logic as distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only when your own data arrived.

1:08:10 LLMs know the future; keep them away from historical data
AI has a two-fold impact on alt data: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs make feature extraction from text easier. But there's a causal trap—using the latest LLM to featurize old documents brings in later events: it knows Enron's eventual fate, and may have seen subsequent revisions of a financial report in its training data. This creates new future information leakage, especially when processing historical data; you must pin down 'which model version at which point in time.'

1:11:26 Stronger models make data cleaning more valuable
A common expectation: as neural networks get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric thinks the opposite: once models can do more themselves, you need less manual feature work, but the data fed in must be more correct. If data isn't point-in-time, leaking future information into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models also have varying tolerance for outliers and dirty patches. Net, cleaning data becomes more valuable, not less.

1:16:34 Usage-based pricing tempts teams to nickel-and-dime
Jane Street runs its data warehouse in its own data center, not purely out of control issues. Eric's observation: moving the same queries to a cloud vendor priced by read volume or compute time gets so expensive you think 'this money could buy a bunch of hardware.' More importantly, the cost model distorts behavior—usage-based pricing makes teams constantly optimize bills and reshape workloads to fit the billing; with self-hosting, cost becomes a one-time hardware investment, and teams spend time on research and queries, not saving money.

item.title: The Most Valuable Step in Writing with AI Isn't the Prompt—It's Turning Editing Feedback into Compound Interest
