item.description: Xiaomi released three Xuanjie chips at once, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture. It's trading resources for time, betting on an on-device AI paradigm shift and vertical integration—but it still lags top-tier chip companies.
item.content:encoded:
Xiaomi released three Xuanjie chips at once, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture. It's trading resources for time, betting on an on-device AI paradigm shift and vertical integration—but it still lags top-tier chip companies.

This episode offers an in-depth analysis of the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It's information-dense, with clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors tracking Xiaomi.

3:02 Chip capability is about system definition, not IP self-reliance
To judge whether a company can make chips, don't just count how many IP blocks it hand-crafts; look at how much system definition power it holds. Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, but system integration and physical implementation are done in-house. Apple and Qualcomm excel at yearly iteration and continuous tape-outs—something latecomers lack. Xiaomi doesn't have a decade to learn slowly, so it chooses an aggressive path, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

6:04 O1's poor energy efficiency stems from a missing shared water tank
The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to spike under heavy GPU load and hurting energy efficiency. An SLC is like a shared water tank in a residential complex: the closer data is to the compute units, the faster the access and the lower the power. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores idle waiting for data—this is the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, split into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduler to handle data consistency and access conflicts.

10:07 ARM's generic bus forced Xuanjie to build its own
ARM's off-the-shelf CHI+CMN solution is too generic, retaining compatibility and redundancy that hinder customization for Xuanjie. The O3 instead develops its own X-Ring unified fabric, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, along with a custom high-speed routing hub and memory controller. This reduces protocol conversion overhead and lets data decide cache placement and paths based on demand. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead drops 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds—32% lower than the O1, even beating Apple's A19 Pro.

12:09 Compute bottleneck shifts from matrix multiplication to vector operations
The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP, etc.—so computation happens where the data resides, reducing data movement. The NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200 TOPS, because Xiaomi judges that the bottleneck for large models is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. The vector unit area is comparable to the Tensor unit, with 6.8 times the multiply-accumulate units of the O1, and it introduces an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

15:11 Chips and models should be co-defined by the same company
Xiaomi partnered with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no accuracy loss, reducing memory bandwidth and capacity needs by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model runs on the O3, with prefill performance up 40% and decode up 45%. This ability to co-define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no need to wait for others to define the model and then adapt a generic chip.

16:11 3nm performance is eked out standard cell by standard cell
The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% higher performance at the same power and 5%-10% lower power at the same frequency. Xiaomi also made extensive process optimizations: self-developed standard cells increased from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip units; compressing the power supply buffer channel lets power and signals route from the middle of modules, boosting transistor density by 5%. The CPU changed from a 4-cluster to a 3-cluster 10-core all-big-core design, with single-core performance up 31% and multi-core up 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

19:13 Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, interconnected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections to achieve high bandwidth with lower energy per bit shift—similar to HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, bandwidth 1.22TB/s, far exceeding the tens of bits of a traditional SoC-LPDDR connection. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each paired with a RISC-V processor for control.

21:17 CXMT's value lies in co-definition, not speed grades
Xiaomi partners with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT offers the 10.667Gbps entry speed grade, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps with wider channels, larger SLC, and a custom memory controller. More importantly, the two companies co-validate and tune from the design stage, jointly defining a Chinese mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and PHY capabilities, earning a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

item.title: Agent Bottlenecks Aren't in Context, but in Memory's Write, Change, Recall, Forget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-cogrev-agent-的瓶颈不在上下文-在记忆的写改召回遗忘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-cogrev-agent-的瓶颈不在上下文-在记忆的写改召回遗忘/
item.description: Uber burning through its token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points to memory as the performance bottleneck—write, change, recall, forget—and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.
item.content:encoded:
Uber burning through its token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points to memory as the performance bottleneck—write, change, recall, forget—and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.

This episode clears hurdles for Agent engineers: how to set chunk size, the 100k vector threshold, who writes and deletes memory; less valuable for those only interested in model progress.

6:32 Database schemas follow the scarcest resource
Pete anchors on E.F. Codd's 1970 relational model paper: when storage was priciest, normalized tables were rational. By MongoDB's 2007 birth, the scarce resource had become time, so the document model deliberately denormalizes, using JSON/BSON to cut disk reads. He also corrects a misread: MongoDB isn't 'schemaless' but 'schema-flexible'—one collection can hold documents of different shapes, letting schema evolve with the product. This design logic shows database schemas should follow whatever resource is scarcest at the time.

16:38 Stuffing context with data degrades quality
Uber burning through its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks is treated as a failed token-maxing strategy. Cost is only half the problem; quality drops too: studies show the first and last few thousand tokens matter most, the middle is mostly noise. This pushes the industry toward 'classified memory'—selecting only the few terms relevant to the current agent loop each round, rather than replaying all history. The key isn't saving money; attention decay inside the context makes selective retrieval a performance issue.

23:21 AI features grow from where customers already hurt
MongoDB's search capabilities grew layer by layer from customer pain: lexical search in 2020 because many were building Lucene themselves; then vector search because vectors are just float arrays, naturally a document field; then combining lexical, vector, and metadata pre-filtering into one hybrid search. In 2025 they acquired Voyage AI to bring embedding models in-house, forming a 'better together' offering. This sequence itself shows infrastructure companies touching AI features usually start from where customers already hurt, not by buying models first and inventing use cases.

40:10 Chunk size tuning should be delegated to the model
RAG's first nagging problem is chunk size: too small, context is insufficient and retrieval quality suffers; too large, storage grows and precision drops, requiring manual trial and error. Voyage's 'contextual chunking' sends the sentence and extra context as two separate strings to the model, which automatically decides the optimal chunk size and returns a single vector. This achieves near-full-context retrieval quality with small chunks and lower storage cost, now in its fourth version. It's a concrete example of moving an engineer's iterative tuning into model weights.

48:20 Embedding models aren't commoditized; choice drives hallucinations
Pete gives two selection thresholds: on scale, you start feeling pain around 100k vectors; on quality, Voyage leads Hugging Face's RTEB benchmark, improving retrieval by up to 14% over other embedding models—a gap that can directly manifest as hallucinations. He reminds that embedding models aren't commoditized—Anthropic doesn't make its own embedding model, so his advice is to use Voyage directly. For many teams, embedding model selection has long been underrated; this segment puts it back at the center of performance and hallucination.

1:01:05 Memory has a half-life and must be actively retired
Why is memory hard? Pete's metaphor: the industry has built databases for sixty years, but agents for about eighteen months. Long-term context strategy is no longer replaying entire conversations; it's recalling best context at query time and writing new facts back to memory after answering; enterprise systems use RBAC to control memory sharing and isolation. He sums up the loop with a colleague's phrase: Write, change, recall, forget. Memory has a half-life—recent info matters more than weeks or months old. This means agent memory must be a first-class citizen, with deliberate writing, updating, and retiring.

1:13:10 First enterprise AI wave lands on employees, not customers
Most Fortune 500 companies Pete talks to are doing employee-facing use cases with humans in the loop. Two reasons: ROI is easier to calculate—these roles already have KPIs—and data breach consequences are lighter; employee data leaks are easier to handle than customer data. Conversely, fully autonomous customer-facing agents are a worse risk-reward bet right now. This provides a coordinate for enterprise AI budget decisions: the first wave is more likely in internal efficiency tools than in robots making final decisions for customers.

1:24:24 Most complex customers aren't in the US but in Mexico City and São Paulo
Pete met this year's most complex customers in Mexico City and São Paulo, and these customers typically assume US competitors are more advanced. He says he sees the opposite. He attributes this to the proliferation of hyperscale data centers and AI services, making geography less important than in the cloud era and leveling global access to technology. This observation suggests country labels are increasingly unreliable for judging whether a company can use cutting-edge AI.

item.title: Fed Chairs Never Lose a Vote: Warsh Talks Against Forward Guidance, but His Path Is Paved for Hikes
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-oddlots-warsh演讲只是b-嘴上反指引-身体要加息/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-oddlots-warsh演讲只是b-嘴上反指引-身体要加息/
item.description: Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, saying he talks against forward guidance but is actually paving the way for rate hikes, and predicts the Fed will hike 75-100 basis points over the next six months.
item.content:encoded:
Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, saying he talks against forward guidance but is actually paving the way for rate hikes, and predicts the Fed will hike 75-100 basis points over the next six months.

Posen is one of the few central bank watchers who dares to say 'fiscal dominance' out loud. This episode has hard judgments on Fed governance risks, Powell's legacy, and AI's employment impact—high information density.

4:07 Warsh didn't say hike, but the whole speech was paving the way
Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, but considering the chaos of the previous two months, it can be treated as a B+. The fourth section systematically lists reasons inflation could persist or even rise, yet never says 'therefore we must tighten.' Posen sees this as deliberate groundwork: if no hike follows, markets will speculate it's a capitulation to Trump's pressure. He himself has been advocating hikes for months because inflation is real. Warsh also reaffirmed the 2% core PCE target and refused to use wage inflation as a forecasting indicator—all mainstream moves.

8:14 Without defining the 'right pace,' returning to target is empty talk
Posen's biggest worry is that Warsh concluded his speech by saying inflation needs to fall in the 'right direction' at the 'right pace,' without ever defining what the right pace is. Without a pace constraint, 'returning to target' is empty talk. From the confirmation hearing, to two press conferences, to the ECB Sintra speech, Warsh has reserved the right to decide 'at the last minute,' refusing to pre-commit to his own indicators. This is close to Greenspan's 1999 style, but Greenspan held it together through personal ability and control of the committee; once you err, the whole credibility collapses.

12:20 A Fed chair never loses a single vote
Posen explains the Fed's committee culture: unlike the ECB, which seeks consensus, the Fed has historically given the chair more power. More critically, there's an unwritten rule—only a few dissent per meeting, and the chair never loses a vote. When Volcker found he might lose, he simply announced it would be his last meeting. This culture leaves the committee with weak ability to correct the chair, so Warsh's 'reserved discretion' style is riskier than he thinks.

19:26 Criticizing the central bank isn't dangerous; making it sell Treasuries is
Posen distinguishes two types of political pressure: ordinary criticism of the central bank is part of the game, and can even help the central bank 'take the blame' when necessary. What's truly dangerous is when a president or Treasury secretary asks the central bank to help sell government debt—the central bank must answer, 'I'm here to help you and your successors sell debt,' and must never manipulate or cheat. Trump's threats to the Fed are far more serious than rhetoric—trying to strip regional Fed presidents of voting rights, disrupt staggered terms, change mandates, and touch the budget directly undermines functional independence.

24:34 The most radical reform might be making the central bank talk less
Posen believes the communications review led by Mervyn King is most likely to produce radical proposals. King himself is a founder of inflation targeting and fan charts, but after retirement he has publicly questioned central banks' forecasting ability and information supply: too much noise makes markets dependent on official guidance, creating moral hazard and bubbles. Peter Fisher similarly argues that central bank 'certainty' makes markets less risk-sensitive. The two may push for reducing rather than increasing information release. Warsh's 'hall of mirrors' metaphor in his speech already admits markets aren't always right.

34:51 Economists entering AI companies lose their independent voice
Posen thinks the rush of economists to AI companies isn't unprecedented—it happened during the internet era—but this time it's more troubling. Companies like Anthropic hire economists partly to design AI transition policies, and these scholars genuinely believe they're doing good. The problem is that once inside, they enter the corporate hierarchy, losing independent voice and freedom to choose topics, and their views are reasonably discounted by outsiders. Posen's hope is that scholars stay at research institutes, earning low six-figure salaries, while retaining public influence.

38:53 AI replacement hasn't happened yet; programmer employment is still growing
Posen says labor market data doesn't yet show AI replacement—even programmer and truck driver employment growth continues. Brynjolfsson's J-curve theory holds that firms need time to reorganize business, and there will be a period of human-AI collaboration first. Garicano's messy jobs theory points out that seemingly automatable jobs actually contain a lot of tacit knowledge and interpersonal relations—truck drivers don't just drive. Large-scale replacement may take about five years, and it will first show up in reduced hiring of young people.

54:13 Rates will be 75-100 basis points higher six months from now
Posen reiterates his earlier forecast of 4% year-end PCE inflation is materializing, with CPI already above 4% early in the year. The bigger issue is inflation inertia: while energy prices may cause a slight dip in the next month or two, core services inflation is sticky, with 3/6/12-month moving averages all rising. He expects the Fed to hike in September or December; if September, December will follow, and six months from now the federal funds rate will be 75-100 basis points higher than now. Only then will inflation begin to truly decline, hovering in the 3.5%-4.5% range in the interim.

item.title: ECT Is Not Torture: 70% Improve, 60% Recover
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-tpwky-ect-不是酷刑-是精神科最有效的疗法之一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-tpwky-ect-不是酷刑-是精神科最有效的疗法之一/
item.description: ECT helps about 70% of patients improve and 60% become symptom-free; it is not the electric torture of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest but the oldest somatic therapy to survive from the slaughterhouse through the anti-psychiatry movement.
item.content:encoded:
ECT helps about 70% of patients improve and 60% become symptom-free; it is not the electric torture of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest but the oldest somatic therapy to survive from the slaughterhouse through the anti-psychiatry movement.

Historical narratives tend toward two extremes: either barbaric torture or miracle cure. This episode puts efficacy, abuse, media amplification, and patient accounts together, showing where the stigma comes from and why it is not the whole picture today.

1:03 The heaviest side effect is not memory loss but stigma
The episode opens with nurse Elan's firsthand account: she had been depressed since childhood, and after medications failed, she chose ECT. She says that after three treatments, colors seemed more saturated and the world became approachable again. Side effects are real: for days after treatment she couldn't name nouns, got lost in familiar neighborhoods, and lost words mid-conversation; long-term memories from before treatment remained but felt like a room that had been rearranged. She states clearly that the heaviest side effect is the stigma surrounding ECT—she worries that sharing her experience will change how others see her, and she believes that stigma is why her doctors did not recommend ECT earlier.

7:53 Fear of ECT is not innate but taught by film and TV
A 2016 global survey of film and television found that 81% of movies and 72% of TV shows portray ECT inaccurately and negatively. In the most famous example, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Jack Nicholson is strapped down and conscious during the shocks, a scene close to torture. A few positive portrayals exist, such as in Homeland and Call the Midwife, but they are rare. The hosts' judgment: public fear of ECT is not凭空产生 but a media stigma reinforced by decades of film and TV; it makes people unwilling even to consider ECT.

13:07 ECT is the most effective psychiatric intervention available
ECT treats severe mental illness like treatment-resistant depression by applying electrical current to the brain to induce a seizure; today it is done under anesthesia and muscle relaxation with strict informed consent. Two figures are often overlooked: about 70% of people improve and about 60% become clinically symptom-free, making it one of the most effective psychiatric interventions available. Compared with patient responses to SSRIs discussed in earlier episodes, it is especially effective for treatment-resistant cases that do not respond to antidepressants alone.

17:09 Electricity is just a tool; the target was always seizure
Shock therapies that emerged in the 1920s were not originally electrical: insulin coma therapy put patients into hypoglycemic coma and convulsions, and Metrosol chemical shock therapy used drugs to induce seizures. Doctors pursued this path because they observed that epilepsy and schizophrenia rarely coexisted, and some catatonic patients improved after spontaneous seizures, so they treated the seizure itself as the key therapeutic ingredient. Cerletti later turned to electricity to find a safer, more tolerable way to induce seizures. Electricity is just a tool; the target is seizure.

22:14 ECT's technical origin is pigs in a slaughterhouse
Cerletti's starting point was the slaughterhouse: workers stunned pigs with electric shocks, and some pigs seized after the shock. In April 1938, a man in Rome with incoherent speech, brought in by police, became the first human subject. No anesthesia, no muscle relaxant; the first two shocks did not induce a seizure. On the third, at a higher dose, a grand mal seizure occurred; the patient stopped breathing and turned cyanotic, then after forty-five seconds took a long breath and recovered. Cerletti later reported 36 cases: 11 complete remissions, 20 improvements, and 5 no change.

31:26 It spread so fast because informed consent did not exist
By 1941, just three years after the first human trial, 42% of psychiatric hospitals in the U.S. had ECT machines. Several reasons explain the rapid spread: it was seen as an improved version of existing shock therapies with a low barrier to entry; doctors were desperate for chronic, severely ill patients; ECT was not the only treatment but often part of a recovery path alongside psychotherapy; early patient reports were generally positive; and there was no informed consent or extended trial period to protect patients. That last point planted the seeds for widespread distrust of psychiatry.

36:34 Using ECT as punishment is not a movie invention
The negative history is not fictional: some institutions used ECT to treat homosexuality or hysteria; 1940s records admit that shock-induced amnesia and disorientation could quiet patients and keep them from disrupting ward order. Such abuses occurred mostly in institutions with fewer resources and more marginalized patients—not in all hospitals—but when exposed they sparked public outrage. The anti-psychiatry movement then framed mental illness itself as social control. The hosts do not excuse these actions but remind us that with few effective drugs and severely overcrowded wards, both doctors and families were trapped in desperation.

42:45 The anti-psychiatry movement forced ECT to prove itself
The anti-psychiatry movement caused ECT use to decline sharply in the 1960s and 1970s, but it also forced ECT to undergo stricter scrutiny and randomized controlled trials. The result: it is the only major somatic therapy from before the era of psychopharmacology that has survived scrutiny. After the 1980s, public accounts by Dick Cavett, Carrie Fisher, and psychologist Norman Endler brought positive narratives back. Memory loss remains a real controversy: research says long-term effects are rare, but some patients feel their experience is not fully captured by measurement tools. The experience cannot be reduced to one star or five stars; it should be neither mythologized nor stigmatized.

item.title: A State Court Authorization Couldn't Beat a Sheriff's 'No Contract'
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-darknetdiaries-持州法院授权测安防-警长却说合同无效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-darknetdiaries-持州法院授权测安防-警长却说合同无效/
item.description: A state court's authorization doesn't cover a county courthouse, turning a commissioned security test into burglary. Even when all charges are dropped, the arrest record stays forever—the justice system can pay damages but can't restore a clean name.
item.content:encoded:
A state court's authorization doesn't cover a county courthouse, turning a commissioned security test into burglary. Even when all charges are dropped, the arrest record stays forever—the justice system can pay damages but can't restore a clean name.

This episode explains the fragility of an 'authorization contract' more clearly than any exploit: the building's owner can override all paperwork, and judicial accountability is nearly blocked by immunity. Security contractors and vendor-side project teams should pause here.

12:07 Verbal agreements are as good as no authorization
The rulebook is only 28 pages, which makes it easy to think the written contract locks everything down. But Gary says the truly detailed agreements were almost all made verbally over the phone; if written down, the contract would be a hundred pages long and no one would sign. That compromise planted a mine: when they later tested the Dallas County Courthouse, the verbal scope didn't cover that building—so procedurally, they walked into a building 'without authorization.' The sheriff's later claim of 'no authorization' wasn't rooted in technology but in a contract that couldn't cover every verbal conversation.

35:18 The building's owner outranks the authorization letter
Before the sheriff arrived, they were confident because the contract clearly stated state court authorization. But the sheriff's reaction was only: they don't own this courthouse, I don't care if you have a contract. Gary and Justin realized that the right to use a building and the right to contract are separate; no matter how formal the state court's contract, it couldn't make entry decisions for the county courthouse's owner. The atmosphere shifted from relaxed to arrest, and they hadn't even worried because no tester in the industry had ever been prosecuted. This time was different.

48:28 The judge heard truth as lies
The judge told Gary, 'You must think I'm stupid'—her reasoning: if the state government had authorized this test, she, as a state employee, would have known; she didn't know, so it could only be a lie. Gary later said this judge, who faced criminals' lies daily, could no longer tell what was true. A reasonable but dangerous logic: in a courtroom full of lies, an alibi-style contract looks even more false. Professional reports and legal procedures were useless in this scenario.

1:03:39 Dropped charges don't erase the record
On January 30, 2020, all charges were dropped, but their criminal records will forever show they were arrested for burglary. Justin said they were deprived of rights without due process—in many U.S. background checks, an arrest record is as visible as a conviction. Dropping charges only means no prosecution; it can't erase the consequences of that arrest: job applications, customs, security clearances—this episode follows them. Winning the criminal fight only won half the battle for their name.

1:17:45 Government immunity blocks accountability for its own mistakes
Seeking accountability was harder than imagined. They wanted to sue the sheriff, the prosecutor, and the judge, but the system threw up two walls: qualified immunity protects individuals acting in official capacity, and sovereign immunity says you can't sue the government without its consent. The state court dismissed first—because the state government was the defendant; the federal court kicked the case back to the state, which dismissed again. This isn't judging a case; it's that the system has no entry point for 'the government was wrong.' The only thing victims can sue is the office, not the person in it; the sheriff personally didn't pay a cent. Judicial checks and balances became a spinning adjective here.

1:31:56 Winning the judicial lottery buys back a sliver of dignity
Almost every wrongful arrest case dies the same way: over 95% are dismissed on qualified immunity, and most of the rest get zero damages or a government victory. Getting more than $50,000 in damages is like winning the lottery, unless you were wrongly held for weeks or months. Gary and Justin were held only one night, but their evidence was airtight, and at arbitration they finally got a rare public statement: it wasn't a question of whether they'd win, but how much. Near trial, the county offered $300,000 each, $600,000 total, to settle. But for them, that money couldn't buy back the half-life already written into their records.

item.title: Residual Connections: The Most Underrated Simple Hack in Deep Learning History
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-welchlabsvideo-残差连接-深度学习史上最被低估的简单-hack/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-welchlabsvideo-残差连接-深度学习史上最被低估的简单-hack/
item.description: ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution isn't deepening networks—it's the residual stream, a working memory that lets models store and edit information, fundamentally changing our understanding of neural networks.
item.content:encoded:
ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution isn't deepening networks—it's the residual stream, a working memory that lets models store and edit information, fundamentally changing our understanding of neural networks.

This episode uses clear animations and experiments to explain why residual connections work, how they led to the Transformer, and evidence that the residual stream acts as working memory. Ideal for anyone wanting to deeply understand the essence of modern AI architectures.

2:07 Deeper networks performed worse
In early 2015, Jian Sun's team used careful initialization to push networks to 30 layers, but performance was worse than 14 layers (error rate 16.59% vs 13.34%). Theoretically, a 30-layer model could achieve at least the same performance as a 14-layer one via identity mapping, but optimizers couldn't find such solutions. This hinted the problem wasn't network capacity but the training process itself.

15:18 Shattered gradients are the root cause
Visualizing the loss landscape revealed that as layers increased, the loss surface for early layers became extremely rugged, with gradient directions as random as white noise—the 'shattered gradients problem.' Gradients are the core signal for learning; once they fail, deep networks can't train effectively.

17:18 Residual connections: an almost absurdly simple fix
Jian Sun's team's solution was laughably simple: between every two layers, add the input tensor directly to the output, creating a skip connection. This provides a direct path for activations and gradients, effectively eliminating the shattered gradients problem. With skip connections, a 74-layer network's accuracy jumped from 38.9% to 72.6%, sweeping major vision competitions in 2015.

20:19 ResNets upended hierarchical representation theory
A Cornell team found that deleting or even shuffling layers in a ResNet had minimal impact on performance. This contradicted the prevailing hierarchical representation theory—which held that each layer builds on the previous, so removing any layer should be catastrophic. It forced a rethink: ResNets might not be learning hierarchical features but iteratively refining a 'residual stream' running through the network.

26:26 The residual stream: modern AI's hidden backbone
Straightening the skip connections reveals an uninterrupted stream from input to output, with each layer making incremental modifications. This 'residual stream' later became the core design of the Transformer and the foundation of modern AI. However, subsequent research showed that ResNets learn both hierarchical representations and refine the residual stream—they can coexist.

29:28 The residual stream is the model's working memory
Meta's team found that in vision Transformers, certain positions in the residual stream have unusually large activations, concentrated in image regions of low importance. They hypothesized the model uses these positions as 'registers' to aggregate global information. Experiments confirmed: embedding vectors from these high-activation positions performed remarkably in image classification (85.2% vs 10.8%), and adding extra 'register tokens' meant the model no longer used image positions.

item.title: Fed Credibility Shatters, Yet Options Markets Shrug
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-excessreturns-美联储信誉崩塌-期权市场却当无事发生/

item.description: The Fed's credibility broke over a single skipped hike, yet options markets price Fed days like any other—the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.
item.content:encoded:
The Fed's credibility broke over a single skipped hike, yet options markets price Fed days like any other—the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.

Three pieces of evidence—sticky inflation, midterm elections, and Fed credibility—point to the same conclusion: volatility is too low, and cheap protection is a mirage. The analytical framework and data are concrete.

3:03 A Fed Without Forward Guidance Is Flipping a Coin
The hosts open by noting the shift: in past FOMC meetings, markets knew the odds with high certainty, but this time the probability of a hike at the next meeting is only 55-45—barely better than a coin toss. Add Warsh's Jackson Hole comments about phasing out forward guidance, and every meeting could become 'see the result, then react.' Rate surprises transmit through debt and leverage to all assets, so volatility needs repricing. The hosts also assert from history: once truly tested by markets, nearly every official eventually caves, so the current promise of 'never pre-committing to market expectations' is itself the variable most worth testing.

17:31 Midterm Election Volatility Priced as an Ordinary Day
Kevin Muir argues that midterm election volatility is severely underpriced. During the 2022 midterms, options markets priced a ±1.8% one-day move in the S&P 500 on voting day; in 2018 it was ±1.25%; now it's only ±0.9%. And this time Trump's approval is at historic lows, and he just spent a prime-time hour talking about 'election fraud,' seemingly laying groundwork to challenge the results. Muir notes: even if you think he's overreacting, that's fine—as voting day approaches, the question of 'will the election be contested' will itself be repriced. With volatility near seasonal lows and implied correlation at historic lows, the odds for long volatility are much better than usual.

23:41 Disinflation Is a Supply Illusion; Demand Hasn't Cooled
Ahan Manon splits PCE components into 'demand-driven' and 'supply-driven.' Currently their contributions are 3.31 vs. 0.38; even if you completely strip out the energy supply shock from Iran tensions, the remaining demand side alone is enough to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target. Historically, demand-driven inflation is slow and persistent, while supply-driven inflation tends to spike quickly and mean-revert within 6 to 12 months. More troubling is the breadth: in recent months, 70% to 80% of PCE components are rising faster than 2%. June saw a negative month-over-month print and July only rebounded 16 basis points, but these short-term cooling effects are almost entirely from the supply side; the demand-driven trend hasn't been interrupted.

34:51 One Hike Could Have Fixed Credibility; He Didn't Do It
Ben Hunt says Warsh hit a 'self-goal' at the post-meeting press conference in July. The newcomer's debut and hawkish inflation rhetoric had repaired the 'Fed credibility' narrative substantially; but the real move was to hike 25 basis points immediately. Just that one hike would have convinced markets that 'he means what he says,' and no repeated hikes would have been needed. Skipping that step reversed the narrative completely: every independent report in the financial press that week said the same thing in different words—'meet the new boss, same as the old boss.' Credibility, once broken, is hard to glue back; August's gold rally is precisely the market's reaction to 'hawkish talk, no action.'

40:13 After the Credibility Hit, Only Jawboning Financial Repression Remains
Ben Hunt lists four pressures the Fed and Treasury must manage but cannot let blow up: the Iran war has no easy exit and oil stays higher for longer; fiscal stimulus fades and tariff pressures return; the insurance sector has a systemic issue with captive insurers being used to take on private investments; and the 10-year and 30-year long-end rates cannot be allowed to rise. Any one of these could be the fuse for the next financial crisis. Managing them requires credibility, which was just wounded, so all policy options are reduced to 'jawboning financial repression'—using statements and intervention to cap yields rather than letting markets price them. His judgment: this operation has no maturity date; it only accelerates.

49:25 Options Markets Treat Fed Meetings as Ordinary Days
Brent Kachuba shows an options term structure with almost no event risk: the 0DTE straddle on the S&P 500 on the day of Warsh's speech is worth only 38 index points; the implied volatility of SPX options expiring August 31 is just 7%, the overall term structure is at 90-day lows, and put open interest is low. He usually avoids trading Fed events because events turn options into a 'tax'—premium is collected before the event, and time value decays once it passes. But this time is special because markets have compressed volatility expectations to near zero and no one is hedging; before Jackson Hole, he bought some 'lottery tickets' with very cheap short-dated put spreads, because if Warsh says one thing the market doesn't like, naked option sellers will get squeezed instantly. After the event passes, that's a better time to follow directional trends.

58:42 Outsourcing Writing to AI Outsources Thinking Too
The closing topic is Druckenmiller's WSJ op-ed: he publicly said it was written by AI, with the simple reason that AI writes better than he does. The hosts argue the core question is whether the views and emotions belong to the author; Druckenmiller's piece reads like his usual gut judgments, with AI only organizing and expressing, so it doesn't constitute deception. Ben Hunt draws the line at writing itself: writing is part of the thinking process—'I write to figure out what I think.' When the text-generation step is outsourced, readers lose an important clue: whether the author actually thought through these words. Obvious AI products are already flooding investment blogs; to judge whether an opinion is reliable, you can't just look at how polished the prose is—you have to ask whether the view has a thinking process behind it.

item.title: China's Economic Peak Has Passed: Credit Dries Up, Deflation Looms
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.description: China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has since declined; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the US has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.
item.content:encoded:
China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has since declined; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the US has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.

To counter the mainstream narrative that 'China's new industries = growth engine,' grounding judgments in verifiable data on credit, special bonds, and demographics; for those looking to update their long-term view of China and the US.

0:05 China has missed its window to overtake the US
Dmitri sets the tone with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined each year since; the US has risen from 24% to about 26%. He concludes that China has almost no chance of replacing the US as the world's largest economy, and the US economic advantage may widen further over the next decade. Logan fully agrees and steers the discussion toward a 'decline, not collapse' framework.

2:11 The root of China's slowdown is the end of credit expansion
Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. After the financial crisis, China added credit equivalent to one-third of global GDP in eight years; credit growth fell from an average of 18% in 2007-2016 to 9% after 2017, and now stands at just over 5%. When credit stops, borrowers can no longer refinance, and investment slows. Official figures still show 5.2% growth in 2023 and 5% in 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 has been only 1.5%-2%, already below the US.

6:14 Using purchasing power parity rewards deflation
Addressing the common rebuttal that 'China has already surpassed the US on PPP,' Logan says PPP comparisons are still meaningful for developing countries but untenable between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP rewards China for producing deflation—the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy appears, yet deflation is precisely the problem. He stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP matters; the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

13:25 Capital controls are not a cure, only a time-buyer
Logan acknowledges that China's capital controls are effective but argues they are not a panacea for massive macro imbalances. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital flow, exchange rate stability, and monetary policy independence can only be achieved two at a time. Capital controls function to delay outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility, and channel outflows into government-visible avenues—Huawei and BYD can expand abroad aggressively, while private firms like HNA in 2016 had their overseas acquisitions halted; this is the two sides of the screening mechanism.

17:35 Credit still subsidizes old industries, not new ones
Logan rebuts the claim that 'credit is shifting to more productive new industries': central bank data shows that loans extended at or below the Loan Prime Rate have risen from over 20% to 59%, indicating banks are continuously subsidizing. The share of special revenue bonds directed to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% in 2021 to 6% in 2025, with the vast majority still flowing to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output table, he estimates that electric vehicles, batteries, AI, and solar together account for about 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in real estate and infrastructure investment is about six times the increase in these new industries.

27:45 Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China will be 'truly finished': the US market has narrowed and transshipment space is limited, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while maintaining its own growth. He warns that the US is wrong to focus only on bilateral deficits—deficits are determined by the savings-investment gap; tariffs merely redistribute deficits, and failing to address the underlying imbalance will only spawn more transshipment trade.

34:58 Without touching taxes, domestic demand won't revive
Logan draws a parallel with Soviet Kosygin reforms: Brezhnev chose to pivot to a technological revolution rather than push reforms that would undermine ideology. To convert savings into consumption, the real lever is tax policy—extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises, and private firms excluded from the financial system. But he considers it almost unimaginable that Xi Jinping would go on TV to announce that 'the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years is no longer applicable'; Beijing's insistence on the 5% growth narrative is partly to undermine export controls and dissuade Western investment in alternative supply chains.

39:00 China in 2035 will look like Japan today
Logan predicts that without major policy shifts, China's economy in 2035 will resemble Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, currency depreciation pressure, and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demographics—China's actual average age at death is 73, and the early PRC baby boom will bring a population decline of 50-60 million over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total population; even maintaining the low birth rate of 7.92 million last year won't stop it. He also notes that the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion per year, about 9.5% of GDP, leaving far fewer resources available than in the past. He concludes that if China truly wins through export share, it will invite stronger political backlash—'winning is losing.'

item.title: Bell Used Einstein's Own Tools to Overturn His Central Argument
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-theoriesofever-贝尔用爱因斯坦自己的工具推翻了他的核心论点/

item.category: Theories of Everything with Curt Jaimungal
item.description: The EPR argument forces you to choose between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism is never a premise but a conclusion that is inferred. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start from here.
item.content:encoded:
The EPR argument forces you to choose between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism is never a premise but a conclusion that is inferred. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start from here.

Maudlin walks from the 1905 photoelectric effect to the 1964 Bell inequality, breaking the EPR argument into steps that can be checked one by one. For those who want to truly understand nonlocality rather than memorize conclusions.

3:05 The father of quantum theory is not Planck but Einstein
Although Planck is usually regarded as the father of quantum theory, it was Einstein's 1905 photoelectric effect paper that actually proposed the quantization hypothesis. Planck only did statistical calculations, while Einstein explicitly argued that energy is transferred in discrete quanta. Maudlin deliberately corrects this historical attribution.

45:32 A single particle is enough to force action at a distance
Einstein's objection at the 1927 Solvay Conference was: if the wave function completely describes a single particle, and the wave spreads in all directions toward the screen, then the particle could act at multiple locations simultaneously. To avoid multiple points of action, one must introduce an instantaneous and global collapse mechanism of the wave function—this is action at a distance. Note, this is not about superluminal signaling.

1:14:50 If the wave function is real, locality has no place to reside
The wave function of a many-particle system is defined on configuration space rather than physical space; for example, a two-particle system is a six-dimensional configuration space. In classical mechanics, configuration space is a mathematical convenience, but if the wave function is taken as fundamental reality, configuration space becomes the physical stage, and the definition of local forces in each small spatial region becomes problematic. This is another layer of Einstein's concern about dynamical locality.

1:31:59 The EPR reality criterion cannot be coherently denied
The EPR reality criterion states: if, without disturbing a system, one can predict with probability 1 the value of a physical quantity, then that quantity corresponds to an element of physical reality. Maudlin emphasizes that this is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. He rebuts common attempts to deny the criterion, arguing that it is analytic and cannot be coherently denied. This sets the stage for the subsequent either-or conclusion.

2:02:26 Either the description is incomplete, or accept action at a distance
Because the reality criterion cannot be denied, the EPR argument forces a choice: either accept that the quantum description is incomplete, or accept that Alice's operation in the lab indeed disturbs the physical state of Bob's particle—that is, action at a distance. Einstein found action at a distance absurd and therefore chose incompleteness. This is the logical exit of the entire EPR argument.

2:10:34 Denying determinism does not escape Bell's conclusion
Maudlin repeatedly emphasizes that in the EPR argument determinism is not assumed but inferred from perfect correlations and locality. He quotes Bell's own words: 'In the limited extent to which determinism plays a role in the EPR argument, it is not assumed but inferred.' Therefore, attempts to escape Bell's conclusion by denying determinism are completely ineffective.

2:43:53 Bohr's famous response was understood by no one
Faced with the EPR argument, Bohr had only two logically possible responses: accept action at a distance, or admit that the quantum description is incomplete. But Bohr chose neither. Maudlin says his response paper is 'a mess' and no one can understand it. He even mentions that in the book edited by Wheeler and Zurek, two pages of Bohr's article are reversed, yet no one noticed, because no one could follow its logic.

2:55:02 Any local theory gives incorrect predictions
Bell's starting point was precisely the EPR paper, yet his conclusion was that Einstein's fundamental claim about 'no action at a distance' was wrong: any local theory fails to make correct predictions. Maudlin calls this a great ironic reversal—Bell used Einstein's own tools to overturn his fundamental argument. This is the true entry point for understanding why Bell's theorem matters.

item.title: The Quantum Endgame Isn't Cleaner Qubits—It's Who Can Use a Phone-Chip Fab Line
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.description: The quantum endgame isn't about whose qubits are cleaner, but who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at a hundred thousand lasers and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.
item.content:encoded:
The quantum endgame isn't about whose qubits are cleaner, but who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at a hundred thousand lasers and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.

The exclusive value is in the second half: HRL paper's CNOT error rate, AI auto-tuning, and FFP's striking scores; the first half's principle explanations are more introductory, and veterans can fast-forward.

0:00 Ion traps and superconductors need miracles; silicon doesn't
To build a hundred-thousand-qubit ion trap, you'd first need to invent the optical miracle of a hundred thousand laser beams; for a million superconducting qubits, you'd need a warehouse-sized cryostat; for a million spin qubits, you just run a standard 300mm silicon wafer through the same lithography equipment TSMC, ASML, and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race isn't single-qubit fidelity, but whether the scaling path already exists in the industrial system.

32:48 Quantum computing is no longer about principles, but engineering
In 2000, DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, aiming to dismiss liquid-state NMR quantum computing. This episode, FFP proposes its own three criteria: qubit quality, control, and scalability with economics. The rest of the episode scores four routes—superconducting, ion trap, neutral atom, and silicon spin—item by item. Laying out the evaluation framework itself tells you: quantum computing has entered the stage of engineering competition, and you can't just talk about principles.

1:24:33 Superconducting isn't a technical failure, but an engineering dead end
Estimates show that a thousand logical qubits require ten million transmon physical qubits. Control line count is limited by the cooling capacity of dilution refrigerators, frequencies are crowded, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconducting only 1/10 on scalability and economics, with a total score of 11/30. This is the first time the show separates 'technically strong' from 'engineering infeasible'; a warehouse-sized refrigerator means even data centers might not fit it.

1:47:08 Ion traps win on coherence time, lose on gate speed
Ion trap coherence times reach ten hours, but gate operations rely on phonons and are limited by Paul trap oscillation frequencies, making them about a thousand times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if ion traps could scale to break encryption, cracking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, while superconducting would take only about eight hours. Long coherence doesn't mean more work per unit time; for practical computing, slow gates are a throughput disaster.

2:03:32 The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor never
A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech, and Qera says ten thousand qubits might break internet encryption, but it would actually take years; even with a hundred thousand physical qubits, under mathematically optimal assumptions, breaking RSA would take about three months. This number strikes both extreme narratives: the quantum threat is not tomorrow, but it is certainly not forever distant. To achieve 'breakable within months' requires qubit count, gate speed, and error correction all to meet the bar simultaneously.

2:50:02 Quantum companies live and die by government contracts
HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research to applied research demanding rapid commercialization; IBM and Intel received support from the CHIPS Act, and ultimately IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the debut of quantum computing's MVP: quantum companies' fates hinge on government contracts, and being acquired isn't failure—it's getting the technology into an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

3:23:10 A million qubits can't be tuned by hand—only by image recognition
Automated tuning becomes key to scaling: a 2023 paper could tune six electrons by hand, but manual tuning of a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition—when scanning voltage, tunneling events appear as stripes; Krishna's team uses DETR combined with ResNet and Transformer to automatically recognize stripes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden premise for why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor fabs: no matter how many qubits, software can auto-align them.

3:32:31 Silicon may not be first, but it will be the last to win
FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (provided isotope enrichment and valley state issues are solved), and 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; neutral atoms score negative 3000. Krishna admits silicon may not be the first route to achieve fault tolerance, but once it does, it will become the final standard—like transistors replacing vacuum tubes—because it's cheap and manufacturable.

item.title: AI Chip Shipments Will Jump an Order of Magnitude: From a Million to 15 Million
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.description: Broadcom's president reveals an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.
item.content:encoded:
Broadcom's president reveals an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.

Broadcom rarely discloses details, but this time it gave three packaging tiers and three shipment volumes, plus a clear take on the HBM bottleneck. For those tracking ASICs and packaging, these 11 minutes are more informative than many long-form analyses.

1:06 Custom chip makers still outsource the last step
Google, Meta, Amazon, and some frontier model companies can have their own chip design teams, define their own architecture and interconnect, but ultimately they still have to 'get the thing built': dealing with foundries and development kits, managing the timing and latency of connections between transistors. Broadcom is the largest of these fee-based back-end design service providers. Clients come to it not just for design capability, but also for a batch of ready-made IP including high-speed I/O, high-speed compute, and memory controllers.

3:09 The most tight-lipped chip company suddenly starts talking
Broadcom is a mystery externally: it has almost no PR department and rarely discloses proactively. Occasionally it releases a Tomahawk network chip or chats with Patrick Kennedy on ServeTheHome. Over the past year, president Charlie has rarely taken the stage at launch events to talk about what Broadcom is doing and why it is expanding its customer base from traditional network chips to custom AI chips. The chart showing three tiers of chips is the clue.

4:09 Today's AI servers are just the smallest of three tiers
Of the three tiers Charlie showed, the leftmost is already shipping in hundreds of thousands of systems, about the size of this Cisco chip on the desk: a central compute die surrounded by four to six HBM modules, packaged using something like TSMC's CoWoS. Broadcom says that over the past year, it has shipped more than one million of these chips to customers. This tier is the reality of today's AI servers.

5:09 Larger packages actually ship in higher volumes
The middle tier is noticeably larger: two to four compute/IO dies surrounded by eight to twelve HBM modules, and AMD's MI455X also fits this design form. Charlie's expected shipment volumes are key: the middle tier is expected to ship 5 million units, and the rightmost tier 15 million. Placed next to 'one million in the past year,' this is not linear growth but an order-of-magnitude jump in shipments for the next generation of custom AI chips.

6:11 The rightmost chip may stack compute dies on compute dies
The rightmost beast: the red parts are eight compute dies arranged in two columns of four, and they are stacked. Charlie lifts the red to reveal purple underneath, which could be SRAM, or SRAM could be on top; if it is compute-on-compute, that effectively equals sixteen compute dies. Each compute die is paired with two HBM modules, so one package contains sixteen HBM modules, with two light-blue IO dies at the top and bottom edges, and openings left at the package edges for optical modules.

7:11 Almost all frontier model companies are building their own chips
Charlie said that of the five most advanced frontier model labs, four are working with Broadcom on custom compute chips. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic define the design they want, Broadcom does the back-end services and interfaces with TSMC, and then partners like Supermicro and WiWynn are brought in for data center scale deployment. This also explains why Broadcom is expanding capacity: it is not only serving traditional network customers but also taking orders from large model companies.

9:11 The bottleneck to scaling may not be packaging but HBM
What may truly be the bottleneck is not packaging but whether there is enough high-bandwidth memory to go around: could a new form between DDR/LPDDR and HBM emerge to fill the gap? Additionally, Broadcom said on stage that it has already deployed a 2nm chip with a partner, slightly smaller than the beast and closer in time. This reminds us that in the coming years, advanced packaging and HBM capacity will be swept up along with custom chip orders.

10:13 The first 2nm custom chip to land may come from Japan
The host pinned down the 'coming soon, smaller' 2nm chip Broadcom mentioned: he asked George from Chips and Cheese, and the two concluded it is Fujitsu's Monaka—a 2nm compute die paired with a 5nm SRAM die, with a central IO die in between. This chip has previously appeared as a mockup or test silicon at several conferences.

item.description: Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.
item.content:encoded:
Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.

This episode has medium information density, but it clearly lays out the rubber trade, indigenous catastrophe, and the beginnings of Manuscript 512; listeners only wanting expedition anecdotes may find the first half's setup a bit long.

3:04 His obsession began with a childhood Roman well
Fawcett was born in 1867. His family was nominally aristocratic, but his father, Edward Fawcett, had squandered the fortune and could only serve as a private assistant to Queen Victoria's son 'Bertie' (later Edward VII). Fawcett described his Torquay childhood as lacking parental affection, which made him introverted. His sister recalled that as a child he discovered a well full of Roman pottery on Halden Moors, and had his siblings lower him down to retrieve the artifacts and take them to a museum. This boldness, stubbornness, and outward-seeking personality later reappeared in his fixation on the occult and the Amazon.

8:13 An officer who held séances still rose to major
In 1901 Fawcett married Nina, and in 1903 their first son Jack was born. That same year he was posted to Spike Island off the south coast of Ireland. Fawcett found the posting dull, so he spent his spare time conducting séances. His interest in the occult was not a fringe hobby; his son Brian later wrote that anyone who sought knowledge beyond the material might be called a mystic. This interest did not hinder his military career—he was promoted to major. This shows that Fawcett's 'rationality' and 'superstition' coexisted, setting the stage for his later credulous belief in Manuscript 512.

10:19 His first Amazon trip was a diplomatic mission, not adventure
In 1901 Fawcett joined the Royal Geographical Society and completed specialized training in boundary demarcation. In 1906 the Society's president, Sir George Goldie, met with him and asked about his knowledge of Bolivia, then told him: border disputes among Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia had escalated because of the rubber trade, and the countries involved would not accept demarcation by any interested party, so the Bolivian government asked the Royal Geographical Society to arbitrate and recommend an officer. For Fawcett, this was a chance to 'escape the monotony of an artillery officer's life'; he was 39, and his wife was pregnant with their second child. The chain of argument here is: rubber's economic value → territorial disputes → Britain as a 'disinterested' third party → Fawcett enters the Amazon as a surveyor. The counterintuitive point is that his initial expedition was not self-directed adventure but commercial and diplomatic arrangement.

14:25 He was attacked everywhere because 90% of natives were already dead
Before he reached South America, the rubber industry had already transformed the region. Figures cited in the episode: before Europeans arrived, the area of present-day Brazil had at least 2,000 indigenous tribes with a total population of about 11 million; in the first hundred years after colonists arrived in the 16th century, 90% of indigenous people died from disease or genocide, and survivors were often enslaved for rubber work. The rubber trade made land extremely valuable, and Europeans moved in and seized indigenous lands, causing natives to view all Europeans as threats—this is the backdrop to Fawcett's encounters with hostility. His own writings also show he was well aware of European colonists' atrocities. This section provides a structural explanation for 'why he was attacked everywhere' and corrects the romanticized narrative of 'explorers in peril.'

17:28 Calling him respectful of natives sets the bar too low
Fawcett's dealings with indigenous people were not solely confrontational. He would insist that he and his companions lay down their arms and show they posed no threat, he learned local languages, and he condemned the earlier European colonists for creating the problems that continued to sour relations. But at the same time, he wrote a great deal that was 'extremely racist' and condescending. The hosts explicitly say that later accounts often describe him as 'respectful of indigenous people,' which is an oversimplification; even if he was 'often better' than his contemporary European explorers, that bar is shockingly low. The value here: many popular narratives today cast Fawcett as an enlightened explorer, and the episode dismantles that myth with specific written evidence, without simplifying his behavior into pure villainy.

19:28 He survived an ambush with an accordion, not a gun
This is one of Fawcett's most famous escape stories. His expedition was ambushed on a river by indigenous archers, and peaceful calls went unanswered. He had his companion Todd sit on a log in the middle of a sandbar with an accordion and start playing, while the others sang loudly and stomped their feet. Soon the hail of arrows stopped, a wide-eyed native peered out from the bushes, and the expedition was welcomed into the village and given help. This example shows Fawcett was not only about force; his problem-solving tools were music and clownish performance. It also shows that his records contain both observations worth taking seriously and plenty of unreliable exaggeration, setting up contrasts with later descriptions of giant anacondas, peanuts, and double-nosed dogs.

25:32 He believed in a lost city because old documents really mentioned it
Before World War I, Fawcett efficiently completed map surveys (often much faster than expected) while becoming increasingly fascinated by claims of lost cities in the jungle. He named the city he sought 'Zed' and located it in the non-coastal southern Brazilian state of Mato Grosso; that area covers about 900,000 square kilometers, is extremely dense forest, and remains one of Brazil's least densely populated regions today, with almost no European entry in the early 20th century. The chain of argument: many 16th- and 17th-century Spanish and Portuguese explorer documents described 'very advanced large cities' → Fawcett believed they were real → he became increasingly obsessed with finding the City of Z.

29:40 The manuscript he believed without reservation may be a hoax
After the war, Fawcett continued studying old documents, most often citing Manuscript 512, held in the National Library of Rio de Janeiro: a Portuguese adventurer's 1753 account of his experiences in the Amazon, sometimes attributed to João de Silvestre de Moraes. Fawcett gave the author the pseudonym Francisco Raposo and wrote that he believed the manuscript's contents 'without reservation,' calling it an 'incomparable story.' However, at the start of the episode the hosts had already foreshadowed that this document 'is very likely a hoax.' So the whole suspense is not 'does the lost city exist?' but rather why a trained geography officer would be so captivated by a possibly forged 1753 record.

item.content:encoded:
Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, and that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations; he also proposes using quantum entanglement entropy instead of thermodynamic entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.

Sean Carroll and Jim Al-Khalili hold opposing views on the arrow of time, and this episode reveals their real points of divergence; the second half also covers mechanisms in quantum biology and a new hypothesis about entanglement entropy.

4:07 The direction of time is built in, not emergent
Jim takes a hard stance: time is real and tangible, part of four-dimensional spacetime, not just something clocks measure. He goes further, saying that the directionality of time is not emergent from directionless fundamental laws but is built into the universe. Sean reminds the audience that this is highly controversial—many physicists think time is just a tool or that its direction is a product of coarse-graining. Jim's intuition is that, viewed from inside the universe, irreversibility is the more fundamental thing.

17:38 No system is isolated, so irreversibility is the norm
The traditional narrative is that fundamental equations like Newton's and Schrödinger's are invariant under time reversal, so the arrow of time must emerge from entropy increase or coarse-graining. Jim turns this around: time-symmetric equations are idealizations because no system is truly isolated—even quantum systems are constantly entangled with their environment. Time-symmetric equations apply only to isolated systems and are special cases of the master equation; in reality, everything exchanges energy and information with its surroundings, and irreversibility is the norm. He admits this is a minority view but thinks it is closer to the real world.

27:50 The special moment must be at the Big Bang, not last week
If you treat the whole universe as an isolated system that also obeys time-symmetric laws, then by the second law, yesterday's entropy should be higher than today's, not lower. The only way out is to push that special moment to the very beginning: the Big Bang. That is the past hypothesis. Jim stresses that this is not an extra assumption but part of the universe's initial conditions, alongside fine-tuning of constants. He agrees with Sean: if you must pick a special moment, the Big Bang is far more reasonable than last week.

31:03 The laws of physics contain no flow of time, yet we feel it
Even if low-entropy initial conditions explain the arrow of time, Sean presses: where do psychological experiences like 'now' and the sense of passage come from? Jim honestly admits that the laws of physics contain no flow of time, yet we feel time flowing. He says this is a gap between physical time and manifest time, and he is not even sure how to articulate it clearly. This candor is more valuable than pretending to have solved it, and it shows the problem of time is far from closed.

45:51 DNA mutations may come from a proton's quantum tunneling
From a nuclear physicist's perspective, Jim presents the most concrete case in quantum biology: the two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds, and a hydrogen atom is essentially a proton. Löwdin proposed in the early 1960s that a proton could quantum-tunnel through the energy barrier to the opposite strand, causing a mutation during replication. Jim's team has done increasingly refined calculations to determine the ratio of tunneling to thermal excitation. He points out that quantum biology is not the old saw that 'atoms are quantum' but asks whether life has evolved to exploit long-lived coherence and entanglement.

1:03:12 A more fundamental version of the past hypothesis uses entanglement entropy
The thermodynamic past hypothesis requires specifying a low-entropy microstate. Jim and philosopher Eddy Chen have tried a more quantum version: assume the universe began in a pure state with extremely low entanglement entropy, with subsystems barely entangled. As it evolves, subsystems become increasingly entangled, and the entanglement entropy of the whole universe rises monotonically. This is conceptually more fundamental than thermodynamic entropy, but Jim admits there are many loopholes—for instance, how finely to partition subsystems. This direction is still unfinished.

1:12:29 After the heat death of the universe, time still passes
Many say time might disappear at extreme scales. Jim counters: even tens of trillions of years from now, when the universe reaches thermal equilibrium and no change can be used to measure time, time still passes. He admits this is not time in the relativistic sense that holds in every reference frame, but it makes time almost like Newton's absolute clock—a real occurrence. For him, even if time emerges from something more fundamental, that does not mean it is not real.
